newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOTOR RACING-HILL ACCLAIMED AS POPULAR CHAMPION.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HILL ACCLAIMED AS POPULAR CHAMPION.

text.p: Damon Hill awoke in his room at the Suzuka Circuit Hotel on Monday with a sore head and the smile of a man who was still struggling to accept that he was the new Formula One world champion.

As his family, friends and team mates chorused in tributes to his success, the 36-year-old Briton prepared for his first day as the title-holder -- and as a driver employed by his new team, TWR Arrows.

This was planned to include a train journey to Tokyo and a long series of television interviews as he attempted to recover from the celebrations which followed his victory and championship success in Sunday's Japanese Grand Prix.

The previous evening Hill had been the toast of a typically wild end-of-season party at the Log Cabin bar in the grounds of the hotel where most of the Formula One paddock appeared to be winding down.

"Obviously, what we had hoped to do was to put two entirely reliable cars out for both drivers so they could go out and battle it out between them," said the Williams team's chief designer Adrian Newey, who worked closely with Hill during his six years with the team.

"So, we were disappointed not to be able to do that. But Damon did a good job. He led from the front and it was a great victory for him. But of course we were disappointed that Jacques (Villeneuve) lost a wheel and retired the way he did."

Newey added that the team had no immediate explanation for the loss of the wheel which flew off Canadian Villeneuve's car 15 laps from the end of Sunday's 52-lap race and bounced ahead of him into the catch fencing.
Villenuve's retirement meant he could no longer win the race and Hill automatically became champion, leaving the Briton just to concentrate on winning his final race for Williams.

Newey confirmed that many of the members of the Williams team were hoping Hill would succeed, at last, in lifting the title and becoming the first son of a former champion to do so. His father Graham won the championship in 1962 and 1968.
"He has been with us for a large number of years and that in itself gained him a lot of respect and affection," Newey said.

"He contributed a lot to the Williams success story, not only in helping us through the dark days in the period after Ayrton Senna's accident in 1994 but also in terms of helping us to develop the car."

Frank Williams, the team chief who told Hill he was no longer required for 1997 when he will be replaced by Heinz-Harald Frentzen of Germany, said: "Damon did a masterful job -- as we've seen many times before.

"He took control of the race and did what he had to do and after four years of hard work, bit by bit, he has got to the top of his mountain. He deserves to be up there and he should have a good look around and take it all in -- I'm sure it's a lovely view."
Williams praised Hill for his dignified behaviour in victory and in defeat, a trait which proved that nice guys can win.
"He is a gentleman and he is without malice," Williams said. "As he was driving round...on the final lap he came on to the radio to the team and he told them: `This is great -- this is yours'.
"He said all the right stuff. And he said it before the race too as we were clearing the grid. He said: `I want you all to know that it was a pleasure working with you this year'."
Hill's departure from Williams will mark the end of an era for the team as they go into their last season with Renault engines in 1997.
Their partnership has been highly successful, enabling Williams to win the constructors' championship five times in the last six years.

They are believed to be keen to link up with the German company BMW as their future engine suppliers but they have also been linked to Honda who on Sunday were also said to be considering a deal with Benetton.
Williams himself said he believed that rival teams -- Ferrari, led by double world champion Michael Schumacher of Germany, McLaren and Benetton -- would be much stronger again next year.

"I am not the sort of person for much celebrating," he said. "I just feel good and enjoy what the team has achieved. But I quickly become severely preoccupied with what's coming down the road...That's just reality."
